title: SC stood tall in crucial cases
primary_topics: Rebuttal of critics' concern about SC softness -- citing historical examples of the Court ruling against the interests of the presidents who appointed its justices
A survey of landmark decisions where the SC voted against Ramos, Estrada, Arroyo, and Aquino administration interests
CJ's confident prediction that justices will uphold the national interest regardless of perceived loyalty to appointing authority
sub_topics: Critics' exhibits: Marcos burial decision, GMA PCSO acquittal, Enrile bail -- same 8-9 justices in majority, same 5-6 in dissent
CJ's standard reply: cannot predict individual votes; disagreements are honest differences; esteem unfettered unless manifest bias or evident error
Ramos era: Imelda Marcos acquittal (Marcos v. SBN, Oct. 6, 1998) -- criticized; but SC voided charter change via initiative (Santiago v. Comelec, March 19, 1997) -- hailed
Estrada era: 13-0 (two abstentions) affirming Estrada ouster, legitimizing Arroyo ascension (Estrada v. Desierto, March 2, 2001)

Arroyo era: Senate v. Ermita (2006) -- EO 464 voided; Bayan v. Ermita (2006) -- calibrated preemptive response voided; David v. Arroyo (2006) -- state of national emergency parts voided; Lambino v. Comelec (2006, 8-7) -- people's initiative trashed
Aquino era: Belgica v. Ochoa (2013) -- pork barrel unconstitutional; Araullo v. Aquino (2014) -- certain DAP practices unconstitutional
History as ultimate judge; Fiat justitia ruat caelum
signature_phrases: when deciding crucial cases under the 1987 Constitution, the Court has stood tall, showing courage, independence and wisdom
Many justices have voted against suits that favor or were initiated by the presidents who appointed them
I just chalk it up to an honest difference of opinions
unless their stance is clearly hobbled by manifest bias, evident error, or similar palpable factors

people: President Fidel V. Ramos (Santiago v. Comelec; Marcos acquittal reproach)
President Gloria Macapagal Arroyo (multiple adverse SC decisions)
President Benigno Aquino III (pork barrel, DAP)
Imelda Marcos (acquitted in Marcos v. SBN)
cases: Bayan v. Ermita (April 25, 2006) -- calibrated preemptive response voided
David v. Arroyo (May 3, 2006) -- state of emergency parts voided
Lambino v. Comelec (Oct. 25, 2006, 8-7) -- people's initiative trashed
Belgica v. Ochoa (Nov. 19, 2013) -- pork barrel unconstitutional
Araullo v. Aquino (July 1, 2014) -- DAP practices unconstitutional

stances.claim: The SC has historically stood tall when deciding crucial cases under the 1987 Constitution -- with many justices voting against the presidents who appointed them, across all administrations from Ramos to Aquino.
The critics' concern about consistent voting blocs in Marcos burial, GMA acquittal, and Enrile bail reflects honest disagreement, but cannot be attributed to manifest bias without more evidence.
stances.rhetorical_move: charitable-interpretation of voting blocs while preserving criticism threshold

stances.claim: Justices know history will ultimately judge them -- law professors and students remember both those who upheld judicial standards and those who betrayed their oaths -- creating an institutional incentive for independence.

notable_anecdotes: President Estrada being 'appalled' that his six appointees joined the 13-0 Estrada v. Desierto decision affirming his own ouster -- the most vivid example of judicial independence over appointer loyalty.
The 8-7 Lambino v. Comelec decision trashing the people's initiative to shift to parliamentary government -- a one-vote margin preserving the presidential system.
CJ's personal admission that he 'occasionally disagrees with friends in the Court' -- establishing his own non-monolithic relationship with colleagues as evidence of genuine independent evaluation.
target_audience: Civic readers anxious about Duterte's forthcoming SC appointments
Constitutional law scholars and law students
Democracy advocates seeking reassurance about institutional resilience

'I just chalk it up to an honest difference' as collegial-charity marker
manifest-bias/evident-error as the threshold for CJ's own criticism
'Fiat justitia ruat caelum' as valedictory moral statement
decision_framework_signals: applies historical-survey-across-administrations to establish baseline SC independence
uses manifest-bias/evident-error threshold as the minimum required for criticism of colleagues
treats historical-accountability as an institutional incentive for independence

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban responds to critics disturbed by the SC's perceived softness -- citing the Marcos burial decision (9-5-1), GMA PCSO acquittal, and Enrile bail -- and worried about Duterte's forthcoming appointments. CJ refuses to predict individual votes or impute bad faith to colleagues unless their stance is 'clearly hobbled by manifest bias, evident error, or similar palpable factors.' He surveys four administrations to show the SC's historical independence: under Ramos, the SC voided the charter change initiative (Santiago v. Comelec, 1997) -- had Ramos appointees voted for it, his tenure might have been extended; under Estrada, his six appointees joined the 13-0 Estrada v. Desierto decision affirming his own ouster; under Arroyo, the SC unanimously voided her EO 464 (Senate v. Ermita, 2006), her calibrated preemptive response policy (Bayan v. Ermita, 2006), parts of her state-of-national-emergency declaration (David v. Arroyo, 2006), and by an 8-7 vote trashed the people's initiative for a parliamentary shift (Lambino v. Comelec, 2006); and under Aquino, the Court unanimously voided the congressional pork barrel (Belgica v. Ochoa, 2013) and declared certain DAP practices unconstitutional (Araullo v. Aquino, 2014). CJ closes: the justices know history will judge them -- law professors and students remember both those who lived up to 'proven competence, integrity, probity and independence' and those who betrayed their oaths. Fiat justitia ruat caelum.
